title: Our Mutual Friend: A Literary Discussion

segments.title: Opening: Money and Mortality in London

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked — a close, searching conversation about one of the strangest and most ambitious novels Charles Dickens ever wrote.
Our Mutual Friend was Dickens's last completed novel, published in 1864 and 1865, and it is a book obsessed with one idea above all others: what money does to people.
What it does to their manners, their marriages, their morals — and ultimately, their souls.
Over this series, we'll be reading the novel closely — passage by passage — with three extraordinary guests who each bring a very different lens to the text.
First, Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic audiobooks than anyone alive.
Oliver hears this novel the way Dickens wrote it — for performance, for the voice, for the room.
Then, Dr. Daniel Rosen — a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power.
Daniel will keep us honest about who the system in this novel serves — and who it destroys.
And finally, Caroline Woodcourt — book critic and lifelong reader of this novel, who first encountered it as a teenager and has returned to it many times since.
Caroline will be our guide to what it actually feels like to read these pages — the music of the prose, the characters who break your heart.
We begin today where the novel begins — with London, with money, and with death.
The thing that strikes you immediately, reading Our Mutual Friend aloud — which I've done, in its entirety, more than once — is how much Dickens is enjoying himself.
There's a glee to the darkness here that you don't quite get anywhere else.
And the Boffins — Mr and Mrs Boffin — arrive in the novel as this magnificent comic gift.
They are good people trying to become fashionable people, and the novel watches their failure with enormous affection.
There's a moment — just a sentence, really — where Dickens delivers the whole verdict on them.
Mr Boffin says to his wife:
"Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!"
And then Dickens adds — and this is the punchline — "It was ruin to Mrs Boffin's aspirations, but, having so spoken, they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair."
That capital U on Unfashionable — Dickens puts it there deliberately.
He's granting them a title — a better one, he implies, than any fashionable society could bestow.
What Oliver is catching there is something so particular to this novel — that tenderness coiled inside the satire.
Because Mrs Boffin's aspirations are being gently mocked, yes.
But what defeats those aspirations is a man telling his wife that he's glad she's his wife.
In a novel full of marriages of calculation and convenience, that is quietly radical.
And the phrase — "this many and many a year" — has this lovely folk-song quality.
It's the rhythm of old loyalty.
I want to hold onto that word — trustworthy — because it's the hinge on which everything turns in this part of the novel.
The old man — John Harmon Senior, the dust contractor, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail as Dickens calls him — this man has spent his life treating everyone as purchasable.
And the one thing his money cannot buy is the Boffins' integrity.
Dickens is very precise about this.
He writes that the old miser had perceived
"the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt."
That is an extraordinary sentence to find in a Victorian novel.
Dickens is saying that the logic of capital — that everything has its price — has a limit.
And what breaks that logic is not heroism or grand rebellion — it's just two faithful servants being decent people across many years.
That's more subversive than it looks.
Daniel's point about purchasability leads me directly to Eugene Wrayburn — one of the great idlers of English fiction.
Eugene is a barrister who does essentially no law, and he has a wonderful explanation for how he arrived at this calling.
His father — referred to throughout with magnificent hauteur simply as M. R. F. — has pre-decided the fate of each child before birth.
Listen to how Eugene tells it — there's a kind of deadpan scaffolding here that's almost architectural.
"When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, 'this,' says M. R. F., 'is a little pillar of the church.'
Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one."
A very shaky one.
Three words.
The entire Victorian establishment — the church, the expectation, the inheritance of duty — skewered in three words.
And what I love is that Eugene tells this story with complete affection for his father — he says so explicitly.
He can't help being amused.
Which is, of course, a very sophisticated defensive manoeuvre.
The eldest brother inherits what the family calls the Family Estate — but Eugene notes the real name for it is the Family Embarrassments.
That tiny irony — the word they use in company versus the truth — is Dickens giving us the whole of English class pretension in a parenthesis.
And Eugene himself — disposed of with highly satisfactory results, as he puts it — is living proof that the system produces people with no idea what they actually want.
Eugene is fascinating to me precisely because he knows all of this and does nothing with the knowledge.
He sees the system perfectly — its absurdity, its arbitrariness — and his response is irony.
A third brother pitched into the Navy because M. R. F. wasn't put out by the surprise of his early arrival.
A mechanical genius decreed for the youngest when he was half an hour old.
These are destinies assigned before the person exists.
That is the class system in its purest form — identity as inheritance, personhood as property.
And Dickens knew it — the man who wrote about the Boffins' inalienable decency knew exactly what it was that the system couldn't buy and couldn't plan for.
Money that cannot buy decency, fathers who design children before they exist, and a couple who ruin their fashionable ambitions with a single tender sentence.
We are very much inside the world of Our Mutual Friend.
In our next segment, we turn to the river — the novel's other great obsession, and the place where its strangest energies collect.

segments.title: The Dust Heaps: Wealth from Refuse

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart piece by piece and asks what it still has to tell us.
Our Mutual Friend is, among other things, a novel obsessed with money — where it comes from, what it does to people, and what people will do for it.
Today we're exploring that obsession through some of the novel's most charged passages — the dust heaps, the river, the grindstone at the keyhole.
With me are three readers who know this novel intimately.
Oliver Trevelyan — actor, writer, and the voice behind more classic novel audiobooks than anyone alive — brings the performer's ear for what the prose wants to do when it's spoken.

Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — and Our Mutual Friend, with its mountains of refuse and its very dead rich men, gives him a great deal to work with.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong reader of this novel, someone who came to it as a teenager and has never quite left.
Daniel, let's begin with you — because the very first pages of this novel give us something extraordinary: a man fishing a dead body from the Thames, and the first thing he does is count the money.
Yes — and Dickens doesn't soften it or hold it at arm's length.
He gives you Gaffer Hexam hauling himself back into the boat, arms wet, hands dirty from a corpse in the river.
And then this single sentence — which is the moral programme of the whole novel, really.
That triple rhythm — chinked, blew, spat — is ritual.
Gaffer is performing a ceremony of acquisition over money stolen from a dead man, and Dickens makes it feel ancient, almost liturgical.
The word 'luck' is doing vicious satirical work there.
In this novel, luck is what the poor call the system when the system happens to let them eat.
What strikes me first is purely musical — the way Dickens has written that sentence for performance.
Three parallel clauses, each with 'once,' building to that hoarse, whispered justification: 'for luck.'
If you read it aloud in any other order, it collapses.
The sequence is locked in — chink, blow, spit — like stage directions that have been made invisible.
And then 'hoarsely said' — not 'said' or 'muttered' but 'hoarsely.'
You hear a man who's been at this a long time, and who's slightly ashamed, and who is doing it anyway.
And there's something almost tender in it, which is what makes it so disturbing.
He washes the money in the same river he just pulled a body from.
There's a terrible domesticity to that — as if this is just housekeeping, just the end of a working day.
And Lizzie is there, watching all of it.
She doesn't speak in this passage — she doesn't have to.
The whole scene is a kind of inheritance being passed on, silently.
That's exactly right — and it sets up the novel's central argument about what wealth actually is.
The Harmon fortune is built on dust — on what the city throws away.
Gaffer's money comes from the dead.
In both cases, the origin of the money is refuse — human or material — and in both cases, the question the novel keeps asking is: what does it do to you to live off that?
Now — on the subject of what wealth does to people — there's a character in this novel who becomes a very unexpected image of that question.
Daniel, you've been looking at Sloppy, and a rather spectacular suit of mourning.
Yes — and I want to say first that this passage is one of the funniest things in the novel.
Which is important, because the comedy is doing political work.
Sloppy has been dressed up by Mrs Boffin — an act of charity and kindness.
Rokesmith personally instructs the tailor to conceal the buttons — to make Sloppy look respectable, to erase the signs of his body.
And the body refuses.
The description of what happens is magnificent — listen to this.
An Argus with a hundred gleaming button-eyes — the poor man's body as a kind of grotesque monster that resists every attempt to dress it into the middle class.
The Argus comparison is extraordinary — because Argus, of course, is the hundred-eyed giant of mythology, the eternal watchman.
So Sloppy, trying to vanish into respectability, accidentally becomes the most conspicuous thing in the room.
And then the rest of the description — the hatband that terminates in a black bunch 'from which the imagination shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted' —
That is comedy at the level of genius.
Not just the thing itself — the hatband — but the philosophical response of imagination and reason to the hatband.
What I love about Sloppy is that the comedy never tips into cruelty — and that's a very difficult line to hold.
We're laughing at the suit, not at Sloppy himself.
Or rather — we're laughing at the whole fantasy that you can dress poverty out of existence.
The suit doesn't fit because the category doesn't fit.
And Dickens ends on that beautiful word: 'Sloppy stood confessed.'
Confessed — as if his body has finally been honest about something that the clothes were trying to suppress.
The body confessing what the system wants hidden.
Daniel, there's another passage I want to bring in — because the novel's treatment of poverty reaches its most devastating pitch with Betty Higden and the river.
This is where the novel stops being satirical and becomes something closer to indictment.
Betty Higden is fleeing the workhouse — fleeing the Poor Law system — and she's dying as she does it.
And Dickens imagines the river itself speaking to her — not as a threat, but as an offer.
The passage describes the young river above the city — still clean, still playful — and then the voice it speaks with.
The Relieving Officer — that's the workhouse official, the embodiment of institutional cruelty — being answered by death itself, which promises to do the job more mercifully.
Dickens is saying, with cold fury, that Victorian welfare had made death preferable to charity.
I find this passage almost unbearable to read, and I mean that as the highest praise.
The river is described first as 'dimpled like a young child' — and that image of childhood innocence is then pressed into the service of death.
There's a pastoral beauty to the language — the weirs, the rushes, the trees — and it makes what the river is offering all the more terrible.
That phrase — 'death in my arms is peacefuller than among the pauper-wards' — is one of the most devastating sentences in all of Victorian fiction.
Dickens made up the word 'peacefuller' — you feel him reaching past correct grammar for the truth.
The repetition of 'Come to me' is the key to reading it aloud.
You have to resist the temptation to make the voice sinister — to play it as a siren's call.
It needs to be genuinely gentle — the most genuinely gentle voice in the novel, which is what makes it so devastating.
Because the horror isn't that death is seducing her.
The horror is that death is being kind — and no living institution is.
That's a very stark conclusion — and it throws into relief one of the novel's stranger subplots, in which money changes hands not through inheritance or theft, but through blackmail.
Daniel — Silas Wegg and the grindstone.
The Wegg subplot is, among many things, a study in how blackmail mimics legitimate economic relations.
Wegg has information — has, in effect, leverage — and he monetises it systematically, the way a landlord monetises property.
But what Dickens gives us in this tiny passage is the theatre of it — the performance.
The sentence reads:
The imaginary grindstone is pure theatrical gesture — Wegg miming the grinding-down of Boffin, who can only stoop at the keyhole and watch.
And then Wegg 'laughed silently, and stumped home' — the most chilling comic exit in the novel.
That 'stumped home' is the punctuation of the whole thing.
Wegg has a wooden leg, so 'stumped' is literal — but it's also the rhythm of a man who has made his point and doesn't need to say another word.
He's content.
Dickens gives you an entire power dynamic in one sentence — and then ends it on a single syllable.
The keyhole detail is wonderful too — Boffin, the man of the house, reduced to peering through his own keyhole at Wegg outside.
The architecture of wealth — the big house — has been turned against its owner.
Which is, of course, exactly what the novel does to wealth throughout — it keeps showing you how easily the house of money becomes a prison.
The house of money as prison — that's a powerful thread.

Before we close this segment, Daniel — there's one final passage I want to bring in, because it moves the question of money somewhere perhaps unexpected: Riderhood, Bradley Headstone, and the vocabulary of debt.
Riderhood is one of those characters the novel uses to expose the logic of capitalism from the inside.
He doesn't have ideology — he has self-interest, purely and nakedly.
He's been watching Bradley Headstone, has gathered his evidence, and now he lays it out — with this extraordinary climax.
The clothes are the evidence — torn, grass-stained, blood-spattered — and Riderhood catalogs them the way a bailiff catalogs assets.
'I've got them, and I've got you' — ownership, pure and simple.
And then: 'I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — I'll be paid for it — till I've drained you dry.'
That triple repetition again — as at the opening of the novel, with Gaffer and his coin.
Dickens keeps returning to the same ritual syntax whenever someone is extracting value from another human being.
That connection between Gaffer and Riderhood is one I genuinely hadn't made before, and it's revelatory.
The novel opens with a man fishing money from a corpse, and it circles back to a man extracting money from a living body — and the prose rhythm is the same.
Dickens is a far more architecturally conscious writer than people give him credit for.
And then the novel puts both of them in the river together, at the end.
Bradley and Riderhood — the man who used money as a weapon and the man who turned that weapon back on him — locked together, dragged under.
The river that whispered to Betty Higden with such terrible tenderness has the last word.
And there, perhaps, is the novel's darkest form of justice — not redeemed by wealth, but reclaimed by water.
But there is, in Our Mutual Friend, another kind of fortune — one that R. Wilfer, in his glowing little speech about Bella, insists is more real than all the dust heaps put together.
That's where we'll pick up — the question of whether this novel truly believes poverty can be a fortune, or whether that's a sentiment it earns.
Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's great final completed novel apart — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we're deep inside one of the novel's most morally intricate arcs: Bella Wilfer's reckoning with money, love, and her own character.
And the strange, prolonged deception that John Harmon — or John Rokesmith — has constructed around her.
To work through all of this, I have three wonderful guests with me.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels on audio than perhaps anyone alive — and nobody hears the music of Dickens's prose more keenly.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as a map of class power — and he will not let us romanticise what is actually quite a disturbing arrangement at the heart of this plot.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and devoted re-reader of this novel, who brings an intimate eye for what moves us and what troubles us on the page.
Let's begin with John Harmon's confession — that extraordinary monologue in which he tries to talk himself through every step of his deception.
Oliver, you've read this passage aloud more than once, I suspect — what strikes you first?
What strikes me first is the rhythm — that extraordinary triple repetition Dickens builds, almost like a legal deposition that keeps catching itself.
Listen to how Harmon actually talks to himself here — he's both prosecutor and defendant, and the prose captures that perfectly.
'I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife.'
That triple 'shrinking' — it's almost a shudder written in syntax.
And then he does what Dickens always does with his most tormented characters — he makes the man check his own arithmetic.
'Now, stop, and so far think it out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.'
It's extraordinary — a man trying to be scrupulously honest with himself inside a tissue of deceptions.
And what breaks my heart a little is that the deception didn't begin from cruelty — it began from fear.
Dickens is meticulous about tracing how it escalated beyond anything Harmon intended.
He sets it out so carefully in the next chapter — let me read just a little of it.

'When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil — never yet for good within his knowledge then — of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.'
That phrase — 'the action for evil, never yet for good' — is Dickens at his most precise and most damning.
The wealth doesn't just corrupt — it has never, within his experience, done anything else.
Caroline is right about the fear — but I want to press on what exactly he was afraid of.
Because when Harmon explains why he staged his own death, it's worth reading very carefully what he actually says.
'The thought entered my head of turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella.'
'Proving Bella.' Two words that carry an enormous amount of ideological weight.
A wealthy man invents his own death to test whether a woman — who has no knowledge of the test — is mercenary enough to be worth marrying.
The dread he names — 'perpetuating the fate that seemed to have fallen on my father's riches' — is real and sympathetic.
But the mechanism he chooses to resolve that dread places him, structurally, in complete power over her.
Daniel, I take the point — but I think Dickens himself is not unaware of the problem.
Look at that passage Caroline was reading — Harmon is trapped in an absolutely impossible double bind.
He can come back to life and buy Bella with the inheritance — or come back and punish her by rejecting it.
Dickens lays out both horns of that dilemma with perfect clarity: 'Was it for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?'
He's writing a novel about money as a moral catastrophe — and the hero cannot step outside that catastrophe simply by wanting to.
And what the novel does so cleverly is parallel Harmon's dilemma with Bella's.
He devises this whole scheme — sailors' disguises, lurking in her neighbourhood — just to see her honestly.
The plot, as Dickens puts it so perfectly drily, was made out of their getting common sailors' dresses and throwing themselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood.
'The plot was made out of our getting common sailors' dresses, and throwing ourselves in Bella Wilfer's neighbourhood, and trying to put ourselves in her way.'
There's something almost farcical about it — two gentlemen playing at poverty, circling a woman who doesn't know she's the subject of an experiment.
And yet — and this is what I keep coming back to — he needed to know whether she was more than the mercenary creature she freely admitted herself to be.
I want to bring in another passage here — because the novel gives us a very sharp image of what money actually does to real people, not just to the plot mechanics of an inheritance.
There's a passage where Lizzie Hexam describes a child to her brother Charley — a child born into absolute degradation.
Listen to how Lizzie puts it — with a simplicity that is far more devastating than any rhetorical flourish.
'This poor ailing little creature has come to be what she is, surrounded by drunken people from her cradle — if she ever had one, Charley.'
'If she ever had one.' That parenthesis is devastating — four words that open into an abyss.
Harmon agonises over whether a rich woman's character has been corrupted by the prospect of money.
Meanwhile, Dickens shows us a child who may never have had a cradle — and that child is simply background texture to the main plot.
That's a provocation worth sitting with — and I don't entirely resist it.
But I'd say Dickens is using that passage to do precisely what Daniel describes — to set the real cost of poverty against Bella's merely theoretical one.
The father in Lizzie's account — falling to pieces, never sober, 'a weak wretched trembling creature' — is what uninherited poverty actually looks like.
Bella's test is a luxury. That's part of the point.
Can we end this thread with Boffin — because Dickens gives us the most delightfully deflating commentary on the whole world of money and charity through him.
That speech about charity books — the patrons and patronesses — it's Dickens at his most comic and most lethal simultaneously.
He just lists them, and the list itself becomes the satire.

'Patrons and Patronesses, and Vice-Patrons and Vice-Patronesses, and Deceased Patrons and Deceased Patronesses, and Ex-Vice-Patrons and Ex-Vice-Patronesses, what does it all mean in the books of the Charities that come pouring in on Rokesmith as he sits among 'em pretty well up to his neck!'
'Up to his neck' — in paperwork, in pretension, in the whole gorgeous absurdity of institutional philanthropy.
And Boffin — this man who actually has the money — just calls it 'stark staring impudence.'
And that's precisely it — Boffin can afford to call it impudence because he's on the inside.
The Vice-Patronesses are merely imitating the logic of a system that Boffin himself embodies.
What Dickens is showing us — through the comedy — is that the entire apparatus of Victorian charity is about status, not about the child who may never have had a cradle.
That brings us to the heart of what makes this novel so permanently alive — it holds the comedy and the tragedy in the same hand without dropping either.
Bella's arc, Harmon's impossible position, the child with no cradle, Boffin's magnificent indignation — they're all facets of the same question Dickens is pressing.
What does money do to a person — and what does it take to refuse its worst terms?
We'll pick up that thread in our next segment — thank you all.

segments.title: A Corpse in the Thames: Harmon's Secret

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show that takes Dickens's last completed novel apart sentence by sentence — and puts it back together with fresh eyes.
I'm your host, and today we're deep in one of the novel's great puzzles: the secret identity of John Harmon — a man pronounced dead who has been walking among the living all along.
Joining me are three exceptional readers of this novel.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has narrated more classic novels than almost anyone alive — he comes to Dickens as a performer, hearing the prose the way it was meant to be heard.
Dr Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads every novel as an anatomy of class power — he will tell us exactly who this inheritance serves and who it crushes.

And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic who has lived with this novel since she was a teenager — she brings the reader's eye, the reader's heart, and very strong opinions about which characters deserve better.
We begin with the Boffins — those golden-hearted people at the centre of this secret — and with the question of what the Harmon fortune has actually cost.
What strikes me every time I return to the Boffin scenes is the sheer generosity of spirit Dickens gives these two people — and how hard he makes you work to believe it.
Because in a novel full of people scheming after the Harmon dust-heap fortune, here are two souls who stood against the old tyrant on behalf of a child they owed nothing to.
And Boffin tells this story to Lightwood with a specificity that is absolutely theatrical — he doesn't generalize, he gives you the hat.
He says, and I love this passage: 'I have seen him, after Mrs Boffin has given him her mind respecting the claims of the nat'ral affections, catch off Mrs Boffin's bonnet —'
'— she wore, in general, a black straw, perched as a matter of convenience on the top of her head — and send it spinning across the yard.'
And then the sentence that stops the room: 'Which dropped her, Mr Lightwood. Dropped her.'
Two words. Full stop. Dickens knows exactly what he's doing.
That repetition — 'Dropped her. Dropped her' — is one of those moments that makes you put the book down just to sit with it.
It isn't melodrama. It's the opposite. It's the understatement of a man for whom the memory is still too immediate to ornament.
Boffin doesn't say 'she fell' or 'she was struck down.' He says 'dropped.' Like a stone. Like a fact.
And what it establishes — quietly, through this one violent domestic image — is the moral foundation on which everything else in the novel rests.
The Boffins suffered for John Harmon before there was any fortune to be had from doing so. That is what makes their goodness legible.
All of that is true, and I don't want to flatten the emotional force of it. But I think we have to ask: what is this scene doing narratively?
Dickens is establishing the Boffins as the only people in this world who are disinterestedly good — so that when John Harmon finally claims the fortune, the transfer can feel clean.
The fortune moves from an abusive patriarch, through the hands of genuinely virtuous people, to a son who was also a victim. The ideological work is immense.
And Harmon himself names it explicitly later, in that magnificent confrontation with Wegg. He says — and this is his voice at its most unguarded —
'I owe everything I possess, solely to the disinterestedness, uprightness, tenderness, goodness — there are no words to satisfy me — of Mr and Mrs Boffin.'
'There are no words to satisfy me.' That parenthesis is everything. The system of language itself buckles under the weight of genuine virtue.
And then he grabs Wegg by the cravat. Which, as a piece of staging, is immaculate.
You get the full moral argument, delivered with absolute clarity — and then the physical punctuation.
Dickens always knew that rhetoric without a body is just hot air. Harmon needs to be furious in his muscles, not just his words.
What moves me about Mrs Boffin's proposal — the adoption plan — is how quietly revolutionary it is within the novel's own logic.
She has come into a fortune built on dust and death. And her first instinct is to redirect it toward a child who has no claim on it whatsoever.
She says — and she qualifies it immediately, with such characteristic modesty —
'Now that he is past all benefit of the money, and it's come to us, I should like to find some orphan child, and take the boy and adopt him and give him John's name, and provide for him.'
'Somehow, it would make me easier, I fancy. Say it's only a whim —'
'Say it's only a whim.' There's such tenderness in that self-deprecation. She doesn't claim virtue. She barely claims intention.
It's a whim that exposes the entire bankruptcy of the inheritance system she has just entered.
The money was meant for John Harmon. John Harmon is dead — or believed to be. So what does the money mean now? What is it for?
Mrs Boffin's answer — find a child, give him the name, make something redemptive out of the whole grim machinery — is more radical than any speech in the novel.
Of course, we later learn that John Harmon is very much alive and has been circulating among them in disguise. Which complicates everything.
And that's where Dickens himself steps forward — which he does, remarkably, in his own voice — to defend the whole conceit.
He says, in what amounts to a direct address to his readers — and I find this absolutely fascinating —

'I foresaw the likelihood that a class of readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he.'
He's saying: I know you guessed. And I meant you to guess. The mystery was never the point.
That is a novelist with enormous confidence in his own design — and perhaps just a touch of defensiveness about the serial readers who wrote in to complain.
What I love about that authorial intervention is that it reframes the whole reading experience retrospectively.
He's asking us to concede him patience — and to trust that the artist knew what he was doing even when the path seemed obscure.
Which, when you put it alongside that moment of Riah spreading a carpet for Lizzie and Jenny on the rooftop — those two women quietly sharing a book above all the city's noise —
— you feel what Dickens's patience was in service of. Small acts of grace, held in trust, waiting to be seen.
That rooftop scene is worth pausing on, because it's easy to read as pure pastoral idyll — and it is beautiful — but it is also profoundly precarious.
Dickens writes: 'Lizzie Hexam and Jenny Wren. For whom, perhaps with some old instinct of his race, the gentle Jew had spread a carpet.'
These women are perched above a city that has no interest in sheltering them. Their garden is chimney-stacks and borrowed books.
Riah's gesture — spreading that carpet — is one of the novel's most quietly devastating acts of solidarity. And the novel barely lingers on it.
And there, in that image — two women sharing a book above London's indifference, a fortune redistributed through love rather than law — we have the novel's deepest argument in miniature.
We'll take a short break, and when we return: the river itself — what it takes, what it gives back, and what Dickens makes of the trade.

segments.title: Schemes and Laughter: The Comic Engine

utterances.text: Welcome to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked, the show where we take Dickens's last completed novel apart — with love — and see what's inside.
Our Mutual Friend is many things: a novel about money, death, identity, and the Thames.
But it is also one of the funniest books in the English language — and that's what we're examining today.
I'm joined by three people who know this novel inside and out.
Oliver Trevelyan is an actor and writer who has voiced more classic novels than perhaps anyone alive — he brings the ear of a performer to every page.
Dr. Daniel Rosen is a cultural historian who reads fiction as an anatomy of class and power — and he finds plenty to work with here.
And Caroline Woodcourt is a book critic and lifelong Dickens reader who cares, above all, about the experience of reading — what moves you, what makes you laugh, what makes you stop.
Today's segment: schemes and laughter — the comic engine of Our Mutual Friend.
Oliver, you've spent your career performing Dickens's prose. Where does the comedy live in this novel?
It lives in the specificity of the language — that's where it always lives with Dickens.
There's a moment early on — Gaffer Hexam dismissing his partner in crime — and the dismissal is written for the voice, not the page.
He says, and I have to read it exactly as it sits on the page —
'Let go. Cast off!'
Two commands. Two beats. Perfectly timed.
That's a man who has rehearsed this speech in his own head and is now performing it with immense self-satisfaction.
The whole speech before it is wonderful too — but those two final words are the punchline, delivered with a theatrical snap.
What strikes me is how Dickens lets the comedy and the menace coexist in that speech.
Gaffer has just threatened violence. And yet the whole thing reads as a performance — almost a pantomime villain's exit.
That tension — between what is genuinely dangerous and what is comic — runs through the whole novel.
But the passage I can't stop thinking about in this context is Wegg's scheme against Boffin.
Because there, the comedy is entirely architectural — it's built into the structure of the prose itself.
Wegg is one of the great comic monsters of all literature — and that passage is his manifesto.
Dickens builds the whole speech on this extraordinary repeated phrase — 'his comrade, brother, and partner.'
Every time Wegg addresses Venus, he adds another title. It's bureaucratic pomposity disguising naked greed.
And then the scheme itself — read the passage and you see the genius of it.
'He considered it plain that such price was stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, Halves!'
He should be kept, Wegg declares, in a state of — and again, verbatim —
'abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his possessions.'
'Abject moral bondage.' Wegg has invented a new form of serfdom. And he's rather proud of it.
The comedy in that passage is real — I laugh every time.
But I'd push us to look at what Dickens is actually satirising there.
Wegg's scheme is a perfect parody of how property and capital actually operate in this novel.
He talks about letting Boffin do all the digging — all the labour — while they extract the profits. That is not a parody of capitalism. That is capitalism.
The comedy functions as a lens. Dickens makes us laugh so that we'll look without flinching.
And notice: Wegg is willing to revise upward — 'It might be more according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds.' He's not even embarrassed. The greed is completely self-legitimating.
And then — and this is what I love about Dickens's comic architecture — Wegg gets his comeuppance in the most theatrical way imaginable.
Sloppy walks in through the folding doors, still wearing the disguise — the dustman's fantail hat — and then simply unties the bandage on his 'broken' head.
The passage is pure stage direction —
'Who, untying his tied-up broken head, revealed a head that was whole, and a face that was Sloppy's.'
That final clause — 'a face that was Sloppy's' — lands like a curtain.
It's perfectly timed. Dickens knows exactly when to stop.
'A face that was Sloppy's.' That is the funniest sentence in a novel full of very funny sentences.
And the word 'beheld' — 'Wegg beheld his persecutor' — Dickens is using epic diction for a man with a wooden leg and a tin of bones.
The comedy of the novel also has a softer register — and I don't want to leave this topic without the scene at Chicksey, Veneering, and Stobbles.
Rokesmith bursting in on Bella and her father — that's pure farce, beautifully modulated.
The narrator builds it with this wonderful escalating structure —
'My dear, dear girl; my gallant, generous, disinterested, courageous, noble girl!'
Five adjectives in a row. He's a man completely overwhelmed by his own feelings and Dickens finds that hilarious and touching in equal measure.
And then Bella lays her head on his breast — and the narrator calls it 'her head's chosen and lasting resting-place.' That's a joke that becomes a vow.
What's interesting to me about that scene is where it happens.
Bella's great romantic moment takes place in a counting-house — surrounded by the brass knobs of a firm's iron safe.
Dickens doesn't let you forget the material world even in the most tender scenes.
The meal they share afterwards — the narrator describes it with this extraordinary image —
'like the supper provided for the three nursery hobgoblins at their house in the forest, without their thunderous low growlings of the alarming discovery, Somebody's been drinking my milk!'
It's a fairy tale of happiness — but grounded explicitly in the absence of threat and discord.
The joy is real. But Dickens insists you understand what it is the joy is free from.
That phrase — 'the two brass knobs of the iron safe, like the eyes of some dull dragon' — that's the whole novel in miniature.
Even here, surrounded by love and a shared meal, the commercial world stares back.
But the passage says the 'uncongenial oddity' of the surroundings only made the meal more delightful.
That is Dickens's comic philosophy in a single sentence. Happiness is more vivid for being improbable.
What I'm hearing is that the comedy in Our Mutual Friend is never merely decorative — it's load-bearing.
The schemes are funny precisely because they are serious. The romance is touching precisely because it's absurd.
We'll be back after a short break to dig deeper into what this novel is really doing with money, dust, and the people who work among both.

segments.title: Atmosphere and Underside: Reading Dickens's London

utterances.text: Welcome back to Our Mutual Friend Unpacked.
We've been circling the great money question at the heart of this novel — who has it, who wants it, and what it does to people.
This segment we're going deeper into Dickens's London itself — the atmosphere, the comedy, the gothic horror, all coexisting on the same page.
Oliver Trevelyan, you've read more Dickens aloud than almost any living person — where do you want to start?
I want to start with the letters — specifically the flood of charitable solicitations that descend on poor Boffin the moment he's marked by good fortune.
Dickens is doing something I find almost miraculously funny here — he's cataloguing the varieties of human greed while pretending to be merely listing correspondence.
And then he produces this specimen — a ducal letter, no less.
"Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet."
Six words — and yet you can feel the weight of it landing on the Secretary's desk, oozing self-importance.

And then we get the full performance from the Duke of Linseed — profound concern for the Family Party Fund, warm personal address to 'My Dear Nicodemus Boffin' — followed, in the postscript, by a three-guinea fee.
Dickens notes, with incomparable deadpan, that the letter is 'lithographed by the hundred.'
What strikes me most about that passage is the rhythm — the way it builds through lists before delivering the satirical sting.
Fifty-seven churches, forty-two parsonage houses, seven-and-twenty organs — Dickens is playing with numbers like a comedian playing with timing.
Each figure is slightly more absurd than the last, and you feel it escalating.
But what I keep returning to is the individual beggars in the next passage — particularly that one devastating comparison.
"they call their scraps documents; but they are, as to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf."
That simile is just extraordinary.
It's comic and brutal simultaneously — there's something almost tender in how precisely it captures the gap between pretension and reality.
I think we have to be careful not to aestheticise what Dickens is doing here — because underneath the comedy there's something genuinely savage.
The individual beggars passage is a taxonomy of desperation — and Dickens renders every type with affectionate mockery, yes, but also with real specificity about what poverty actually produces.
The beggars of punctual business-habits, for instance — threatening to be 'cold in death' at a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday if no postal order arrives.
On the surface it's comic, but what it actually describes is a system that has driven people to perform their own suffering as a transaction.
And who is the actual villain in the charity satire?
Not the beggars — the Duke of Linseed, with his lithographed letter, extracting three guineas from a man newly rich while dressing it up as honour.
Daniel is absolutely right — though I'd say Dickens has the rare gift of making you laugh at something and feel the horror of it at exactly the same moment.
And there's a dark parallel here with Wegg's discovery of that second will — another piece of paper, another document, carrying enormous consequence for Boffin's fortune.
Wegg reads it out with his characteristic blandly buoyant manner — and the contents are bracingly cold.

"Inasmuch as he has never made friends, and has ever had a rebellious family, he, John Harmon, gives to Nicodemus Boffin the Little Mound, which is quite enough for him, and gives the whole rest and residue of his property to the Crown."
'Which is quite enough for him' — said of a fortune.
That's old Harmon's voice from beyond the grave, still contemptuous, still controlling — even in death, he gets the last mean word.
There's something in that will that echoes across the whole novel — this idea that wealth doesn't liberate, it just redistributes the cruelty.
Old Harmon had a rebellious family because he was a tyrant — and yet the will reads as if the family wronged him.
Which brings me to something at the opposite extreme of the novel's register — the Bradley Headstone passage.
Because if the Boffin letters are London's comic face, this is its gothic face — and Dickens moves between them without the slightest awkwardness.
The description of Bradley sitting through the night is almost unbearable to read slowly.

"Rigid before the fire, as if it were a charmed flame that was turning him old, he sat, with the dark lines deepening in his face, its stare becoming more and more haggard, its surface turning whiter and whiter as if it were being overspread with ashes, and the very texture and colour of his hair degenerating."
'The very texture and colour of his hair degenerating' — that detail is almost clinical in its precision.
It's as if the despair is a physical process, consuming him from inside, like fire consuming ash.
Bradley Headstone is perhaps the most frightening figure in the whole novel for me — because his tragedy is entirely structural.
He's a man who has hauled himself up from nothing through sheer effort, through schoolmastering, through the suppression of everything instinctive in himself.
And then that suppressed self breaks free in a way that destroys him.
The charmed flame image is doing something very specific — this is a man being punished by a system that offered him just enough education to feel his own imprisonment acutely.
He can't unsee what he knows about himself, and he can't escape it.
That image of the fire turning him old — for a performer it's extraordinary material, because Dickens is rendering an internal state as pure visual spectacle.
The prose is doing the work of an actor's face in close-up — the deepening lines, the whitening surface, the hair losing its very substance.
And the genius of it is that Riderhood is just — watching.
The vulture keeping vigil while the man burns.
What I find most remarkable about this novel, hearing you all talk about it, is exactly that range — from lithographed ducal letters to a man being consumed by despair before a fire.
London in Our Mutual Friend is simultaneously the funniest and the most terrifying place in Victorian fiction.
In our next segment, we'll turn to the Thames itself — the river that gives the novel its deepest rhythms and its darkest secrets.
We've spent this episode tracing the currents that run through Our Mutual Friend — money, identity, who gets counted and who gets discarded.
I want to close by asking each of you: what does this novel ultimately say about transformation — personal and social?
Oliver, let's begin with you — you've been listening to this novel's rhythms all episode.
There's a passage I keep coming back to — and it has nothing to do with any of our central characters.
It's the train crossing the river.
Dickens describes it like this:

"the train rattled among the house-tops, and among the ragged sides of houses torn down to make way for it, and over the swarming streets, and under the fruitful earth, until it shot across the river: bursting over the quiet surface like a bomb-shell, and gone again as if it had exploded in the rush of smoke and steam and glare."
That's modernity, isn't it?
Violent, magnificent, indifferent — blasting through everything that was there before.
And then Dickens pulls back and compares the river's course to Father Time himself — inevitable, unstoppable, unimpressed by human commotion.
For all its social comedy, this novel knows it's writing about mortality — and time — and what we leave behind.
That passage is extraordinary — but I want to pair it with something much smaller in scale, because the two belong together.
Dickens introduces Twemlow — a gentleman of good family and absolutely no means — and describes him as a piece of dining furniture.
The exact words are:
"Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state."
A human being — rendered as an object for other people's use.
And the more socially useful he becomes, the further he is pushed from the centre of any table he sits at.
That's the novel's central thesis about class, delivered as a joke about furniture — and it lands precisely because it is funny.
The comedy is the critique.
"The comedy is the critique" — I want that on a wall somewhere.
And notice what Dickens does with Twemlow's address — he's stored over a livery stable-yard in Duke Street when not in use.
Warehoused, like furniture, between dinner engagements.
The brilliance is that Twemlow never quite understands what's being done to him — which is, of course, the most devastating detail of all.
What strikes me about Twemlow is that by the end of the novel, he finds his voice.
That dining-table extension who could be pulled out further and further from the centre — he speaks with moral clarity when it counts.
That's transformation, and it matters precisely because it's so quiet.
But then I think of Charley Hexam — someone who could have transformed, who had every reason to, and chose not to.
There's a moment where Charley confronts Bradley Headstone after the attack on Eugene, and it's almost unwatchably selfish.
He tells Bradley:
"you are in all your passions so selfish, and so concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought on me."
The accusation is correct — and yet Charley is its perfect mirror image.
He can see selfishness in Bradley with surgical precision and remain entirely blind to his own.
That's the novel refusing easy consolation — not everyone transforms.
Charley is the novel's most uncomfortable character to sit with, precisely for that reason.
He has clawed out of poverty through education — which the novel elsewhere values — and yet that very clawing has hollowed him out.
Dickens is asking something hard: can you escape a system without being reshaped by it in the worst possible way?
Charley's answer, unfortunately, is no.
And yet the river keeps moving.
What I love about that train passage is the end of it — Dickens describes the river's many "turnings and doublings" that the train crosses with contempt.
But the river still reaches the sea.
The novel is full of characters who turn and double and seem to go nowhere — and then arrive somewhere entirely unexpected.
That's what makes it inexhaustible as a reading experience.
The comedy is the critique, the furniture is the human being, and the river always reaches the sea — I think that's as fine a summary of Our Mutual Friend as I've heard.
Oliver Trevelyan, Daniel Rosen, Caroline Woodcourt — thank you for spending this time in Dickens's extraordinary, inexhaustible novel.
For listeners joining us for the first time: go back and read it.
For those who know it: read it again.
It will be different this time — it always is.

c9:p28.text:
‘Yes; and it’s pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin,’ said her
      husband, ‘and it’s been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a
      year!’ It was ruin to Mrs Boffin’s aspirations, but, having so spoken,
      they sat side by side, a hopelessly Unfashionable pair.
c9:p28.summary: Mr Boffin lovingly affirms his wife's moral character, but Dickens narrates that their virtuous intentions doom their social aspirations to fashionability.
c9:p28.best_quote: Yes; and it's pleasant to know that you are Mrs Boffin, and it's been a pleasant thing to know this many and many a year!

c9:p30.text:
Through his most inveterate purposes, the dead Jailer of Harmony Jail had
      known these two faithful servants to be honest and true. While he raged at
      them and reviled them for opposing him with the speech of the honest and
      true, it had scratched his stony heart, and he had perceived the
      powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to
      the attempt. So, even while he was their griping taskmaster and never gave
      them a good word, he had written their names down in his will. So, even
      while it was his daily declaration that he mistrusted all mankind—and
      sorely indeed he did mistrust all who bore any resemblance to himself—he
      was as certain that these two people, surviving him, would be trustworthy
      in all things from the greatest to the least, as he was that he must
      surely die.
c9:p30.summary: Dickens explains that old John Harmon, despite his misanthropy and greed, respected the Boffins' moral integrity so deeply that he named them in his will as trustees of his fortune.
c9:p30.best_quote: he had perceived the powerlessness of all his wealth to buy them if he had addressed himself to the attempt

c12:p25.text:
‘Perfectly so, believe me; and with every sentiment of affectionate
      deference towards M. R. F. But if he amuses me, I can’t help it. When my
      eldest brother was born, of course the rest of us knew (I mean the rest of
      us would have known, if we had been in existence) that he was heir to the
      Family Embarrassments—we call it before the company the Family
      Estate. But when my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, “this,”
       says M. R. F., “is a little pillar of the church.”  Was  born, and became a
      pillar of the church; a very shaky one. My third brother appeared,
      considerably in advance of his engagement to my mother; but M. R. F., not
      at all put out by surprise, instantly declared him a Circumnavigator. Was
      pitch-forked into the Navy, but has not circumnavigated. I announced
      myself and was disposed of with the highly satisfactory results embodied
      before you. When my younger brother was half an hour old, it was settled
      by M. R. F. that he should have a mechanical genius. And so on. Therefore
      I say that M. R. F. amuses me.’
c12:p25.summary: Eugene recounts how his father pre-arranged careers for all his siblings (eldest as heir, second as clergyman, third as naval officer, himself as barrister and married man, youngest as mechanical genius), all with varying degrees of failure.
c12:p25.best_quote: When my second brother was going to be born by-and-by, "this," says M. R. F., "is a little pillar of the church." Was born, and became a pillar of the church; a very shaky one.

c1:p9.text:
It was not until now that the upper half of the man came back into the
      boat. His arms were wet and dirty, and he washed them over the side. In
      his right hand he held something, and he washed that in the river too. It
      was money. He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon
      it once,—‘for luck,’ he hoarsely said—before he put it in his
      pocket.
c1:p9.summary: Gaffer emerges from the water with money in his hand, which he washes, chinks, blows upon, and spits on 'for luck' before pocketing it.
c1:p9.best_quote: He chinked it once, and he blew upon it once, and he spat upon it once,—'for luck,' he hoarsely said—before he put it in his pocket.

c27:p51.text:
The consideration of Mrs Boffin had clothed Mr Sloppy in a suit of black,
      on which the tailor had received personal directions from Rokesmith to
      expend the utmost cunning of his art, with a view to the concealment of
      the cohering and sustaining buttons. But, so much more powerful were the
      frailties of Sloppy’s form than the strongest resources of tailoring
      science, that he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way
      of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a
      hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators. The
      artistic taste of some unknown hatter had furnished him with a hatband of
      wholesale capacity which was fluted behind, from the crown of his hat to
      the brim, and terminated in a black bunch, from which the imagination
      shrunk discomfited and the reason revolted. Some special powers with which
      his legs were endowed, had already hitched up his glossy trousers at the
      ankles, and bagged them at the knees; while similar gifts in his arms had
      raised his coat-sleeves from his wrists and accumulated them at his
      elbows. Thus set forth, with the additional embellishments of a very
      little tail to his coat, and a yawning gulf at his waistband, Sloppy stood
      confessed.
c27:p51.summary: Sloppy's new black suit is a comedic disaster: buttons gleam like eyes, the hatband is absurdly fluted, his sleeves ride up and trousers bag at the knees, and his coat has a yawning gap at the waistband.
c27:p51.best_quote: he now stood before the Council, a perfect Argus in the way of buttons: shining and winking and gleaming and twinkling out of a hundred of those eyes of bright metal, at the dazzled spectators.

c41:p7.text:
In those pleasant little towns on Thames, you may hear the fall of the
      water over the weirs, or even, in still weather, the rustle of the rushes;
      and from the bridge you may see the young river, dimpled like a young
      child, playfully gliding away among the trees, unpolluted by the
      defilements that lie in wait for it on its course, and as yet out of
      hearing of the deep summons of the sea. It were too much to pretend that
      Betty Higden made out such thoughts; no; but she heard the tender river
      whispering to many like herself, ‘Come to me, come to me! When the cruel
      shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! I
      am the Relieving Officer appointed by eternal ordinance to do my work; I
      am not held in estimation according as I shirk it. My breast is softer
      than the pauper-nurse’s; death in my arms is peacefuller than among the
      pauper-wards. Come to me!’
c41:p7.summary: Dickens uses vivid description of the river landscape to imagine the Thames itself whispering an invitation to the suffering and desperate—offering death as a kinder relief than institutional charity.
c41:p7.best_quote: Come to me, come to me! When the cruel shame and terror you have so long fled from, most beset you, come to me! This time Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an
      imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it

c53:p125.summary: Wegg silently mines turning a grindstone at the keyhole while Boffin watches helplessly from within; Wegg then laughs and departs.
c53:p125.best_quote: This time Silas made no reply, but laboured with a will at turning an imaginary grindstone outside the keyhole, while Mr Boffin stooped at it within; he then laughed silently, and stumped home.

c65:p84.text:
‘But two could play at your game,’ said Riderhood, snapping his fingers at
      him half a dozen times, ‘and I played it long ago; long afore you tried
      your clumsy hand at it; in days when you hadn’t begun croaking your
      lecters or what not in your school. I know to a figure how you done it.
      Where you stole away, I could steal away arter you, and do it knowinger
      than you. I know how you come away from London in your own clothes, and
      where you changed your clothes, and hid your clothes. I see you with my
      own eyes take your own clothes from their hiding-place among them felled
      trees, and take a dip in the river to account for your dressing yourself,
      to any one as might come by. I see you rise up Bradley Headstone, Master,
      where you sat down Bargeman. I see you pitch your Bargeman’s bundle into
      the river. I hooked your Bargeman’s bundle out of the river. I’ve got your
      Bargeman’s clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained
      green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the
      blows. I’ve got them, and I’ve got you. I don’t care a curse for the
      T’other governor, alive or dead, but I care a many curses for my own self.
      And as you laid your plots agin me and was a sly devil agin me, I’ll be
      paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—I’ll be paid for it—till
      I’ve drained you dry!’
c65:p84.summary: Riderhood describes in detail how he witnessed Bradley's transformation, possession of the bloody bargeman's suit, and his intent to drain Bradley financially until completely ruined as punishment.
c65:p84.best_quote: I've got your Bargeman's clothes, tore this way and that way with the scuffle, stained green with the grass, and spattered all over with what bust from the blows. I've got them, and I've got you.

c49:p74.text:
‘And therefore—and therefore,’ the cherub went on in a glowing
      voice, as Bella’s hand stole gradually up his waistcoat to his neck, ‘this
      mercenary young person distantly related to myself, refused the price,
      took off the splendid fashions that were part of it, put on the
      comparatively poor dress that I had last given her, and trusting to my
      supporting her in what was right, came straight to me. Have I led up to
      it?’
c49:p74.summary: R. Wilfer blesses the engagement, declaring his profound admiration for Bella's choice to accept poverty with Rokesmith rather than wealth, and affirming that her choice is the truest fortune.
c49:p74.best_quote: The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did well! The mercenary young person distantly related to myself, did not trust to me in vain! I admire this mercenary young person distantly related to myself, more in this dress than if she had come to me in China silks, Cashmere shawls, and Golconda diamonds. I love this young person dearly. I say to the man of this young person's heart, out of my heart and with all of it, "My blessing on this engagement betwixt you, and she brings you a good fortune when she brings you the poverty she has accepted for your sake and the honest truth's!"

c30:p7.text:
‘When I came to England, attracted to the country with which I had none
      but most miserable associations, by the accounts of my fine inheritance
      that found me abroad, I came back, shrinking from my father’s money,
      shrinking from my father’s memory, mistrustful of being forced on a
      mercenary wife, mistrustful of my father’s intention in thrusting that
      marriage on me, mistrustful that I was already growing avaricious,
      mistrustful that I was slackening in gratitude to the two dear noble
      honest friends who had made the only sunlight in my childish life or that
      of my heartbroken sister. I came back, timid, divided in my mind, afraid
      of myself and everybody here, knowing of nothing but wretchedness that my
      father’s wealth had ever brought about. Now, stop, and so far think it
      out, John Harmon. Is that so? That is exactly so.
c30:p7.summary: John Harmon explains that he returned to England reluctantly, conflicted about his inherited wealth, fearful of a mercenary marriage, and anxious about his own character.
c30:p7.best_quote: I came back, shrinking from my father's money, shrinking from my father's memory, mistrustful of being forced on a mercenary wife

c31:p1.text:
He went over it all again. He had lapsed into the condition in which he
      found himself, as many a man lapses into many a condition, without
      perceiving the accumulative power of its separate circumstances. When in
      the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never
      yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his
      father’s wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of
      his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few
      hours or days, it was to involve in it only the girl so capriciously
      forced upon him and upon whom he was so capriciously forced, and it was
      honestly meant well towards her. For, if he had found her unhappy in the
      prospect of that marriage (through her heart inclining to another man or
      for any other cause), he would seriously have said: ‘This is another of
      the old perverted uses of the misery-making money. I will let it go to my
      and my sister’s only protectors and friends.’ When the snare into which he
      fell so outstripped his first intention as that he found himself placarded
      by the police authorities upon the London walls for dead, he confusedly
      accepted the aid that fell upon him, without considering how firmly it
      must seem to fix the Boffins in their accession to the fortune. When he
      saw them, and knew them, and even from his vantage-ground of inspection
      could find no flaw in them, he asked himself, ‘And shall I come to life to
      dispossess such people as these?’ There was no good to set against the
      putting of them to that hard proof. He had heard from Bella’s own lips
      when he stood tapping at the door on that night of his taking the
      lodgings, that the marriage would have been on her part thoroughly
      mercenary. He had since tried her, in his own unknown person and supposed
      station, and she not only rejected his advances but resented them. Was it
      for him to have the shame of buying her, or the meanness of punishing her?
      Yet, by coming to life and accepting the condition of the inheritance, he
      must do the former; and by coming to life and rejecting it, he must do the
      latter.
c31:p1.summary: Rokesmith justifies his original deception as harmless, traces how it spiralled beyond his control, and wrestles with the impossible choice between disgracing Bella or deceiving the Boffins.
c31:p1.best_quote: When in the distrust engendered by his wretched childhood and the action for evil—never yet for good within his knowledge then—of his father and his father's wealth on all within their influence, he conceived the idea of his first deception, it was meant to be harmless, it was to last but a few hours or days.

c30:p22.text:
‘I have checked the calculation often, and it must have been two nights
      that I lay recovering in that public-house. Let me see. Yes. I am sure it
      was while I lay in that bed there, that the thought entered my head of
      turning the danger I had passed through, to the account of being for some
      time supposed to have disappeared mysteriously, and of proving Bella. The
      dread of our being forced on one another, and perpetuating the fate that
      seemed to have fallen on my father’s riches—the fate that they
      should lead to nothing but evil—was strong upon the moral timidity

When I devised this story, I foresaw the likelihood that a class of
      readers and commentators would suppose that I was at great pains to
      conceal exactly what I was at great pains to suggest: namely, that Mr John
      Harmon was not slain, and that Mr John Rokesmith was he. Pleasing myself
      with the idea that the supposition might in part arise out of some
      ingenuity in the story, and thinking it worth while, in the interests of
      art, to hint to an audience that an artist (of whatever denomination) may
      perhaps be trusted to know what he is about in his vocation, if they will
      concede him a little patience, I was not alarmed by the anticipation.

On this head, Silas Wegg had much to say. Silas had to say That, he would
      beg to remind his comrade, brother, and partner, of the impressive
      passages they had read that evening; of the evident parallel in Mr
      Boffin’s mind between them and the late owner of the Bower, and the
      present circumstances of the Bower; of the bottle; and of the box. That,
      the fortunes of his brother and comrade, and of himself were evidently
      made, inasmuch as they had but to put their price upon this document, and
      get that price from the minion of fortune and the worm of the hour: who
      now appeared to be less of a minion and more of a worm than had been
      previously supposed. That, he considered it plain that such price was
      stateable in a single expressive word, and that the word was, ‘Halves!’
      That, the question then arose when ‘Halves!’ should be called. That, here
      he had a plan of action to recommend, with a conditional clause. That, the
      plan of action was that they should lie by with patience; that, they
      should allow the Mounds to be gradually levelled and cleared away, while
      retaining to themselves their present opportunity of watching the process—which
      would be, he conceived, to put the trouble and cost of daily digging and
      delving upon somebody else, while they might nightly turn such complete
      disturbance of the dust to the account of their own private investigations—and
      that, when the Mounds were gone, and they had worked those chances for
      their own joint benefit solely, they should then, and not before, explode
      on the minion and worm. But here came the conditional clause, and to this
      he entreated the special attention of his comrade, brother, and partner.
      It was not to be borne that the minion and worm should carry off any of
      that property which was now to be regarded as their own property. When he,
      Mr Wegg, had seen the minion surreptitiously making off with that bottle,
      and its precious contents unknown, he had looked upon him in the light of
      a mere robber, and, as such, would have despoiled him of his ill-gotten
      gain, but for the judicious interference of his comrade, brother, and
      partner. Therefore, the conditional clause he proposed was, that, if the
      minion should return in his late sneaking manner, and if, being closely
      watched, he should be found to possess himself of anything, no matter
      what, the sharp sword impending over his head should be instantly shown
      him, he should be strictly examined as to what he knew or suspected,
      should be severely handled by them his masters, and should be kept in a
      state of abject moral bondage and slavery until the time when they should
      see fit to permit him to purchase his freedom at the price of half his
      possessions. If, said Mr Wegg by way of peroration, he had erred in saying
      only ‘Halves!’ he trusted to his comrade, brother, and partner not to
      hesitate to set him right, and to reprove his weakness. It might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Two-thirds; it might be more
      according to the rights of things, to say Three-fourths. On those points
      he was ever open to correction.

But no one knows so well as the Secretary, who opens and reads the
      letters, what a set is made at the man marked by a stroke of notoriety. Oh
      the varieties of dust for ocular use, offered in exchange for the gold
      dust of the Golden Dustman! Fifty-seven churches to be erected with
      half-crowns, forty-two parsonage houses to be repaired with shillings,
      seven-and-twenty organs to be built with halfpence, twelve hundred
      children to be brought up on postage stamps. Not that a half-crown,
      shilling, halfpenny, or postage stamp, would be particularly acceptable
      from Mr Boffin, but that it is so obvious he is the man to make up the
      deficiency. And then the charities, my Christian brother! And mostly in
      difficulties, yet mostly lavish, too, in the expensive articles of print
      and paper. Large fat private double letter, sealed with ducal coronet.
      ‘Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. My Dear Sir,—Having consented to preside
      at the forthcoming Annual Dinner of the Family Party Fund, and feeling
      deeply impressed with the immense usefulness of that noble Institution and
      the great importance of its being supported by a List of Stewards that
      shall prove to the public the interest taken in it by popular and
      distinguished men, I have undertaken to ask you to become a Steward on
      that occasion. Soliciting your favourable reply before the 14th instant, I
      am, My Dear Sir, Your faithful Servant,  Linseed . P.S. The Steward’s fee is
      limited to three Guineas.’ Friendly this, on the part of the Duke of
      Linseed (and thoughtful in the postscript), only lithographed by the
      hundred and presenting but a pale individuality of an address to Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, in quite another hand. It takes two noble Earls and a
      Viscount, combined, to inform Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, in an equally
      flattering manner, that an estimable lady in the West of England has
      offered to present a purse containing twenty pounds, to the Society for
      Granting Annuities to Unassuming Members of the Middle Classes, if twenty
      individuals will previously present purses of one hundred pounds each. And
      those benevolent noblemen very kindly point out that if Nicodemus Boffin,
      Esquire, should wish to present two or more purses, it will not be
      inconsistent with the design of the estimable lady in the West of England,
      provided each purse be coupled with the name of some member of his
      honoured and respected family.

c17:p5.text:
These are the corporate beggars. But there are, besides, the individual
      beggars; and how does the heart of the Secretary fail him when he has to
      cope with  them!  And they must be coped with to some extent, because they
      all enclose documents (they call their scraps documents; but they are, as
      to papers deserving the name, what minced veal is to a calf), the
      non-return of which would be their ruin. That is to say, they are utterly
      ruined now, but they would be more utterly ruined then. Among these
      correspondents are several daughters of general officers, long accustomed
      to every luxury of life (except spelling), who little thought, when their
      gallant fathers waged war in the Peninsula, that they would ever have to
      appeal to those whom Providence, in its inscrutable wisdom, has blessed
      with untold gold, and from among whom they select the name of Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire, for a maiden effort in this wise, understanding that he
      has such a heart as never was. The Secretary learns, too, that confidence
      between man and wife would seem to obtain but rarely when virtue is in
      distress, so numerous are the wives who take up their pens to ask Mr
      Boffin for money without the knowledge of their devoted husbands, who
      would never permit it; while, on the other hand, so numerous are the
      husbands who take up their pens to ask Mr Boffin for money without the
      knowledge of their devoted wives, who would instantly go out of their
      senses if they had the least suspicion of the circumstance. There are the
      inspired beggars, too. These were sitting, only yesterday evening, musing
      over a fragment of candle which must soon go out and leave them in the
      dark for the rest of their nights, when surely some Angel whispered the
      name of Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, to their souls, imparting rays of hope,
      nay confidence, to which they had long been strangers! Akin to these are
      the suggestively-befriended beggars. They were partaking of a cold potato
      and water by the flickering and gloomy light of a lucifer-match, in their
      lodgings (rent considerably in arrear, and heartless landlady threatening
      expulsion ‘like a dog’ into the streets), when a gifted friend happening
      to look in, said, ‘Write immediately to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire,’ and
      would take no denial. There are the nobly independent beggars too. These,
      in the days of their abundance, ever regarded gold as dross, and have not
      yet got over that only impediment in the way of their amassing wealth, but
      they want no dross from Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire; No, Mr Boffin; the
      world may term it pride, paltry pride if you will, but they wouldn’t take
      it if you offered it; a loan, sir—for fourteen weeks to the day,
      interest calculated at the rate of five per cent per annum, to be bestowed
      upon any charitable institution you may name—is all they want of
      you, and if you have the meanness to refuse it, count on being despised by
      these great spirits. There are the beggars of punctual business-habits
      too. These will make an end of themselves at a quarter to one P.M. on
      Tuesday, if no Post-office order is in the interim received from Nicodemus
      Boffin, Esquire; arriving after a quarter to one P.M. on Tuesday, it need
      not be sent, as they will then (having made an exact memorandum of the
      heartless circumstances) be ‘cold in death.’ There are the beggars on
      horseback too, in another sense from the sense of the proverb. These are
      mounted and ready to start on the highway to affluence. The goal is before
      them, the road is in the best condition, their spurs are on, the steed is
      willing, but, at the last moment, for want of some special thing—a
      clock, a violin, an astronomical telescope, an electrifying machine—they
      must dismount for ever, unless they receive its equivalent in money from
      Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire. Less given to detail are the beggars who make
      sporting ventures. These, usually to be addressed in reply under initials
      at a country post-office, inquire in feminine hands, Dare one who cannot
      disclose herself to Nicodemus Boffin, Esquire, but whose name might
      startle him were it revealed, solicit the immediate advance of two hundred
      pounds from unexpected riches exercising their noblest privilege in the
      trust of a common humanity?

      parallel still held; for, it always happened that the more Twemlow was
      pulled out, the further he found himself from the center, and nearer to
      the sideboard at one end of the room, or the window-curtains at the other.
c2:p2.summary: Twemlow, a man of good family connections, is introduced through an extended metaphor comparing him to a dining table that the Veneerings manipulate for social purposes.
c2:p2.best_quote: Being first cousin to Lord Snigsworth, he was in frequent requisition, and at many houses might be said to represent the dining-table in its normal state.

c57:p86.text:
‘When I speak of my sister, I devoutly wish that you had never seen her,
      Mr Headstone. However, you did see her, and that’s useless now. I confided
      in you about her. I explained her character to you, and how she interposed
      some ridiculous fanciful notions in the way of our being as respectable as
      I tried for. You fell in love with her, and I favoured you with all my
      might. She could not be induced to favour you, and so we came into
      collision with this Mr Eugene Wrayburn. Now, what have you done? Why, you
      have justified my sister in being firmly set against you from first to
      last, and you have put me in the wrong again! And why have you done it?
      Because, Mr Headstone, you are in all your passions so selfish, and so
      concentrated upon yourself that you have not bestowed one proper thought
      on me.’
c57:p86.summary: Charley recounts how his favor and support for Bradley have been repaid with violence that justifies Lizzie's opposition and damages Charley himself.
